name: Wikidata data model (statements, qualifiers, references, ranks)
what: Official spec of Wikidata's model: items and properties, statements with qualifiers and references, three ranks (preferred, normal, deprecated), unknown and no-value markers.
why_it_matters: The only open all-domain graph that already carries per-claim sources and rank-based conflict handling at scale; the template to copy or beat for people and orgs.
numbers: ~123.6M content pages and 2.56B page edits per Special:Statistics (captured undated); ~13,972 properties, ~76% external identifiers (data model page); ~68% of statements referenced (2021 paper, secondary).
ui_notes: Statement cards show value, qualifiers and references; ranks are not visually distinguished in the web UI (open Phabricator task, secondary source).
note: item > statement(property, value, qualifiers, references, rank); no statement-level truth flag, ranks instead | check: Wikidata Data_model and Statistics pages: 13,972 properties, 76% external identifiers, 123,624,278 items, 2,556,092,845 edits (all match). The 68% referenced statement share was not checked.

name: Wikidata at query scale (WDQS, QLever mirror, graph split)
what: How Wikidata is queried at scale: Blazegraph WDQS being replaced by QLever candidate; scholarly items split into a second query service on 9 May 2025; weekly RDF dumps.
why_it_matters: Shows the practical ceiling of one monolithic RDF store and the fix (split subgraphs plus a faster engine), which we would need for an all-of-history people+org graph.
numbers: ~17B triples (2022 workshop paper); 20B triples in QLever's full-Wikidata benchmark; ~1B triples/year growth (Wikidata team, 2023); WikiCite data >50% of triples (2025 CEUR paper).
ui_notes: Public QLever endpoint lags the live site by up to a week because it loads weekly dumps.
note: RDF triples in Blazegraph/QLever; split by subgraph (scholarly vs rest)

name: Factoid prosopography model (KCL, Bradley, Byzantine tradition)
what: Prosopography modelled as a collection of source-level assertions (factoids): each factoid is a spot in a source saying something about a person, linked to sources, persons, places, possessions and classification schemes.
why_it_matters: Direct ancestor of claim-level people graphs; keeps conflicting sources side by side instead of forcing one biography per person, which is the exact behaviour a 'every human ever' graph needs.
numbers: Tens of thousands of factoids per project (KCL page); Prosopography of the Byzantine World core ~60,000 factoids, ~7,500 seals (older Oxford DH page).
ui_notes: Users assemble their own narrative from assertions; no per-person article is authored.
note: factoid = source + assertion about person(s); FPO is an OWL/RDFS ontology on GitHub

name: SNAP:DRGN (Standards for Networking Ancient Prosopographies)
what: KCL-based pilot that defines minimal RDF standards for person data in ancient prosopographies and gives each identified person a URI so name references across datasets link to one person, Pelagios-style.
why_it_matters: Concrete crosswalk-ID pattern: many prosopographies (PIR, LGPN, Trismegistos, Papyri.info) share URIs for the same person rather than merging records.
numbers: Not stated on the intro page; PIR persons in PIR2 A-R and PIR1 S-Z carry SNAP IDs (open-epihub and Digital Classicist pages).
ui_notes: Scholarly, no end-user UI; API-level linking.
note: person URI per identified person; minimal RDF person core; crosswalk by URI

name: Trismegistos People (TM People)
what: Papyrological person database for non-royal individuals in Egypt 800 BC to AD 800, with separate PER (person) and REF (attestation) tables that link persons to the documents that mention them.
why_it_matters: Clean two-table model of person vs. attestation, with IDs that cross-reference many other ancient-person databases; a working example of a merged-but-linked identity layer.
numbers: 380,676 person records and 555,414 attestations (about-page snippet; an older ISAW index gives 458,045 attestations); fetch of the page failed on certificate, so counts are from search snippet.
ui_notes: Search by name, place, date; each person has a TM ID and per-attestation document links.
note: PER table (person) + REF table (attestation to document); TM IDs crosswalk to other DBs

name: Prosopography of the Byzantine World (PBW, KCL)
what: Byzantine prosopography built from factoids (one assertion per source mention), restructured mid-1990s from print articles into a data-first resource; covers AD 1025-1180 in its current scope.
why_it_matters: Proof that a factoid-first database can run for decades and be re-used; a template for the source-first design of a people+orgs graph.
numbers: Core ~60,000 factoids, 2,774 narrative units, ~7,500 seals (older Oxford DH description); current person total not found.
ui_notes: Browse by person page assembled from factoids; each factoid cites its source.
note: factoid rows (source, person, place, possession) plus classification schemes

name: Prosopographia Imperii Romani (PIR) online and data repo
what: Print prosopography of Roman elite (1st-3rd century) with an online name index and API; PIR2 A-R and PIR1 S-Z carry unique IDs; a GitHub data repo is listed under CC BY 4.0.
why_it_matters: Shows the limit of a print-first prosopography: biographical content withheld for publisher reasons, only names and citations open. Good lesson on licensing the data layer separately from the text.
numbers: Scope of Roman elite for 300 years; record count not confirmed in this slice.
ui_notes: Name search returns names and bibliographic citations; full biographies are not public.
note: name + bibliographic citation per person; SNAP IDs; partial JSON API

name: VIAF (Virtual International Authority File)
what: OCLC-run cluster service that matches national authority files (LC, GND, BnF and others) and merges their records into a super-cluster per person or organisation, without replacing the source records.
why_it_matters: The largest working example of a crosswalk-first identity layer for people and corporate bodies: source IDs stay, a derived cluster ID sits on top, and the crosswalk is rebuilt on a schedule.
numbers: Cluster run monthly; many national agencies contribute (count not confirmed in this slice); LC-GND-OCLC proof of concept 2003, BnF joined 2007.
ui_notes: Public cluster page per VIAF ID with source-record links and name variants.
note: source record IDs crosswalk to derived cluster ID; monthly re-cluster can split or merge IDs

name: FamilySearch Family Tree (one shared world tree)
what: Single shared genealogy tree in which each person is one profile; duplicates are merged person-by-person with field-level choice, possible-duplicate hints, safeguards and an Undo Merge after each merge.
why_it_matters: The largest single tree of people with live merge practice; its merge rules (block living/deceased, different sex, parent-child) and change-log reasons are directly reusable for a people graph.
numbers: ~1.74 billion names as of July 2025 (FamilySearch); no official duplicate count found.
ui_notes: Merge page shows recommendation levels (no obvious problems, potential, not recommended, unable to merge), Not a Match marking, and reason statement required.
note: one profile per person; merge = survivor + field picks + change log; Undo Merge | check: FamilySearch blog: about 1.74 billion names as of July 2025; matches row.

name: WikiTree (one profile per person, trusted-list merges)
what: Open genealogy wiki with one profile per person; duplicate profiles are merged only when both owners agree, and the merge is irreversible once completed.
why_it_matters: Shows the governance cost of merges: owner consent plus irreversibility keeps data clean but slows throughput; contrast with reversible judgement-graph merges.
numbers: Count not checked in this slice.
ui_notes: Merge flow asks owners to agree, then lets the editor pick which field values to keep.
note: one profile per person; consent-gated, irreversible merge

name: Geni World Family Tree (matching and merge centre)
what: Commercial genealogy site aiming for one World Family Tree; duplicate matching across user trees plus MyHeritage smart and record matching; merges need profile owners' approval.
why_it_matters: Demonstrates a matching pipeline fed by multiple trees and records; the merge bottleneck is owner response, not matching accuracy.
numbers: Count not confirmed in this slice; blog-era (2015) reports only.
ui_notes: Merge Center lists suggested matches; users must add enough generations for matching to fire.
note: per-user trees merged into a world tree via matching + owner approval

name: GLEIF Golden Copy (Level 1 identity, Level 2 ownership, reporting exceptions)
what: Free, daily-issued legal-entity dataset: Level 1 LEI records (who is who), Level 2 relationship records (direct and ultimate parents), and Level 2 reporting exceptions explaining missing parents, all with delta files.
why_it_matters: The cleanest open org-identity plus ownership graph with a daily update cadence; the reporting-exception file is a good model for recording why a link is absent, not just that it is missing.
numbers: Three Golden Copy sets issued daily plus four delta files (8h, 24h, 7d, 31d); record count not shown on page; LEI-level ownership only, not natural-person UBOs (Open Ownership).
ui_notes: Downloadable CSV/XML; LEI lookup API links records to Level 2 data where available.
note: entity record + relationship record + exception record; daily full + delta | check: GLEIF download page: three Golden Copy sets issued daily plus four delta files at 8 hours, 24 hours, 7 days and 31 days earlier; matches row.

name: OpenCorporates (statement model for companies and officers)
what: Largest open company registry aggregator across ~140 jurisdictions; the API reference says the data moved from a per-item datum model to a statement model with finer provenance, with existing datums migrated to statements.
why_it_matters: Live example of an org graph that switched to per-fact provenance mid-life; the migration is the thing to learn from, not just the scale.
numbers: 220M+ companies and 310M+ officers (OpenCorporates knowledge base); 143M companies and 128 jurisdictions in 2018 blog post.
ui_notes: Company page with jurisdiction code, officers, filings; open-data licence for non-commercial use.
note: company + officer + jurisdiction; datum migrated to statement with source

name: ROR (Research Organization Registry) data dumps on Zenodo
what: Open registry of research organisations with stable ROR IDs, released as versioned JSON (schema v1 and v2) and CSV dumps; the JSON is the format of record.
why_it_matters: A small, curated, versioned org registry with a stable ID and a published schema switch, good for the org axis of the graph; it is organisations only, no people.
numbers: 120,196 organisations in v1.74 (24 Nov 2025); 119,173 in v1.72; the Zenodo record URL was matched to a release in search snippets, not verified.
ui_notes: Searchable registry on ror.org; API default moved to v2 July 2025 and v1 deprecated Dec 2025.
note: org record with stable ID, versioned JSON dump, schema v2 switch

name: CIDOC-CRM actor model (E39 Actor, E21 Person, E74 Group, E82 Actor Appellation)
what: ISO standard event-centric cultural-heritage ontology: people and groups are actors, names are appellations attached to actors, and life facts (birth, death, formation) are events rather than attributes.
why_it_matters: The standard vocabulary for a person as an actor with event-based life history and appellation-based names; the event-not-attribute choice is the one to copy for dated facts about people and orgs.
numbers: Standard; no scale claim (not a dataset).
ui_notes: Ontology only; used in LINCS and museum graphs.
note: actor + appellation + event (birth, death, formation) with P-properties

name: Nanopublications (assertion + provenance + publication info, Trusty URIs)
what: Scholarly format where each claim is a named graph of three parts: the assertion, its provenance, and publication info, made immutable with a hash-based Trusty URI.
why_it_matters: The strongest published pattern for statement-level provenance and immutability; it is the closest thing to per-claim sourcing done as a standard, and it gives a way to cite a single claim.
numbers: Growing uptake across life sciences (DisGeNET published as nanopublications); no global count in these results.
ui_notes: Not a UI product; nanopub servers and a nanopub viewer exist.
note: named graph: assertion, provenance, pubinfo; Trusty URI for immutability

name: W3C PROV-O (provenance ontology)
what: W3C recommendation for provenance: Entity, Activity, Agent; wasGeneratedBy, wasDerivedFrom, wasAttributedTo, plus qualified influence classes.
why_it_matters: The standard vocabulary to reuse for who-said-what, but it has no native per-triple provenance; the page says a Bundle is the nearest tool, so statement-level sourcing must be built on top.
numbers: Standard; no scale claim.
ui_notes: Ontology only.
note: entity/activity/agent; bundles for named provenance sets; no triple-level provenance

name: Splink (probabilistic record linkage, Fellegi-Sunter)
what: Python library (UK Ministry of Justice) for probabilistic deduplication and linking of records without shared IDs, unsupervised EM training, blocking rules and clustering of match pairs into entity IDs.
why_it_matters: The most practical open tool for the entity-resolution step of a people+org graph at laptop scale; it runs on DuckDB and scales to Spark for 100M+ records.
numbers: ~1M records linked on a laptop in about a minute; 100M+ on Spark (project page); one user reports 30M addresses in under 5 hours on Databricks.
ui_notes: Interactive comparison and cluster charts in the docs.
note: pairwise match probability then clustered entity IDs; EM-trained m/u parameters | check: Splink docs: links a million records on a laptop in approximately one minute; DuckDB or Spark for 100+ million records; matches row.

name: nomenklatura (OpenSanctions entity resolution and statements framework)
what: Framework behind OpenSanctions: entities stored as statements (one value per property, with dataset and date), judgements stored as positive or negative pairs, canonical IDs minted per positive decision, merges computed at export from the judgement graph.
why_it_matters: The closest open design to what we need: source-level statements, reversible merges by changing judgements (not data), and a blocking-based candidate list; the basic OpenSanctions facts are already held, this row is for the merge and statement design.
numbers: 130,000 entities would mean ~17B pairwise comparisons; 34,600 manual decisions in 8 weeks (31,000 positive); ~300,000 implied negative pairs.
ui_notes: Analysts compare pairs side by side in a text tool and record same/different.
note: statement (prop, value, dataset, date) + judgement graph + canonical ID; merge is a view | check: OpenSanctions 2021 blog: 130,000 entities, ~17B pairwise comparisons (130k x 130k cross-product), 34,600 manual decisions, 31,000 positive, ~300,000 negative pairs; all quoted correctly.

name: YAGO 4.5 (Wikidata with schema.org upper taxonomy and SHACL)
what: Knowledge base derived from Wikidata that puts Wikidata classes under a schema.org-style upper taxonomy (Person, Organization, Event, Place, etc.) with SHACL constraints for cleaning and reasoning.
why_it_matters: Shows how to clean Wikidata's class soup into a typed person/org layer with logical constraints; directly relevant to typing a people+org graph.
numbers: 49M entities and 109M facts (official page); paper arXiv 2308.11884 (SIGIR 2024).
ui_notes: Downloads as Turtle and N-Triples with SHACL schema files.
note: Wikidata-derived; schema.org upper classes; SHACL disjointness; facts without per-claim rank

name: Freebase (Metaweb; retired 2016)
what: Open, graph-shaped knowledge base of topics, types and properties with user-editable types under folksonomy rules; Google bought Metaweb in 2010 and announced the shutdown in Dec 2014, closing 2 May 2016 with Wikidata as the successor.
why_it_matters: The closest historical attempt at a community-curated all-of-world graph; its death is the cautionary case in the lessons section of the notes.
numbers: ~44M topics and 2.4B facts (January 2014, Wikipedia citing the Freebase page).
ui_notes: Freebase UI had topic pages and an MQL query explorer; closed with the API and widget.
note: topic + type + property graph (graphd, MQL); no per-fact sources; restricted schema edits

name: Google Knowledge Graph (last public scale figure, 2020)
what: Google's proprietary graph of entities and facts behind search panels; partly fed by Freebase and Wikipedia; no public implementation documentation.
why_it_matters: Shows the scale the commercial side reached, and that its inner data model is closed; it cannot be copied directly but sets the scale benchmark.
numbers: 500B facts about 5B entities (May 2020, Google); 570M entities and 18B facts at 2012 launch; third-party 2022 estimate 9.25B entities (unofficial).
ui_notes: Search knowledge panels and cards.
note: closed entity + fact graph; no public per-fact source model

name: Diffbot Knowledge Graph (people and organisations, auto-extracted)
what: Commercial knowledge graph built by automated extraction from the web, with person and organisation entities and facts; claims refreshes every few days and a changelog of enrichment.
why_it_matters: Proof that automated web extraction can produce a people+org graph at billions of entities; the open question is whether per-fact sources are exposed (vendor marketing only here).
numbers: April 2021 whitepaper: 1.3B+ person entities, 715M+ organisation entities, 242M+ articles; 2024 Workspace listing: 20B+ entities and 2T+ facts; refresh every 3-5 days (vendor claim).
ui_notes: API and Excel/Sheets add-ins; no open dump found.
note: entity + facts from web extraction; closed; no per-fact source exposed in these pages

name: OpenAlex author object (person profile as derived set of works)
what: Person-level profiles built by disambiguating name strings from works; the profile is a set of linked works, identity fields (ORCID, observed ORCIDs) and affiliations are derived from authorships, and fixes are made by changing the works.
why_it_matters: A clean derived-profile design: the person is a view over sourced works, so bad merges are fixed upstream; relevant for a people graph where facts come from documents.
numbers: Only ~1 in 10 profiles has a primary ORCID (page); counts and disambiguation method on linked pages not read.
ui_notes: API only; affiliations cover ~10 years, full history via works grouped by year.
note: person = derived view over works; ids (openalex, orcid, observed_orcids); updated_date stamp
